title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0) that embeds a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (270 paired tasks), gpt-5-mini as the generator (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet emulator as semantic ground truth, the frozen run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task evaluated in both arms). Observed outcomes: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); no verifier rejections occurred and no repairs were invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). We (1) report the executed, artifact‑anchored conditional result, (2) document the preregistration ↔ executed sampling semantics mismatch that makes the preregistered power calculation inapplicable, (3) provide precise artifact pointers and SHA‑256 hashes (see Disclosure) and a minimal deterministic recipe to re‑run the archived harness under the original independent‑sampling estimand, and (4) discuss operational and validity implications for GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction: Motivation and question. Automating intent→configuration translation with generative models promises major NetOps productivity gains but raises safety and correctness concerns when stochastic generators emit commands that violate invariants (reachability, redundancy, failover). Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) systems interpose deterministic validators between generation and deployment to constrain stochasticity. Our preregistered study asked: does embedding a deterministic formal network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded GVR loop increase the proportion of unsafe or incorrect LLM outputs detected/rejected and improve bounded repair success relative to a generate‑only baseline (primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline)? Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, fully archived paired experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fba...) that executed a frozen plan and recorded all raw transcripts, validator traces, and hashes. (2) An artifact‑anchored conditional empirical outcome (shared_initial_candidate semantics) showing no marginal verifier effect for the chosen task bank and generator. (3) Transparent documentation of a decisive design mismatch (preregistered power assumed independent per‑arm generation; execution evaluated a shared generated candidate per pair), with an explicit minimal recipe (manifest edits) to re‑run the archived harness under the original independent‑sampling estimand. (4) A discussion of operational implications and reproducibility artifacts.
sections.related_work: Positioning. GVR and generate‑then‑verify architectures have been advocated in regulated code generation and AI‑assisted development [Cadenas et al., Convergent Correctness; doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899] and in LLM‑agent toolchains. Formal network verification (NetKAT/weighted NetKAT and domain decision procedures) provides deterministic oracles for many network properties and has been used as a safety layer in intent‑based and intent⇢configuration pipelines [Suárez Acevedo et al.; doi:10.1145/3808318]. Recent NetOps/LLM surveys and RAG/agent reviews (OpenAlex entries W4414359351, W4400072049, W4386722061) motivated our task design and the choice to combine synthetic intent tasks, an LLM generator, and an emulator+deterministic verifier. Gap. Prior work provides conceptual GVR recipes and case studies; however, reproducible, preregistered experiments that (a) fix generation and verifier budgets, (b) archive full provider traces and hashes, and (c) report inferential statistics for a defensible paired estimand are lacking. Our study fills that experimental and archival gap for a narrowly scoped conditional design.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The preregistration (netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fba...) fixed the research question, primary/secondary estimands, task bank structure, generator family, verifier identifier, retry/stopping rules, and analysis methods before observing outcomes. Key preregistered elements executed without post hoc changes: task bank size and composition (270 paired tasks: 3 vendor‑style syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 per cluster = 270), adapter family (hosted_netops_gvr_v1), declared generator gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...), deterministic verifier deterministic_netops_validator_v5, emulator harness (Dockerized Kathará/Mininet images archived in execution/*), and analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1. Execution sampling semantics (decisive). The frozen execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each task the pipeline generated one candidate and that identical candidate was evaluated in both arms (baseline and guarded). This is recorded in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json) and is the proximate cause of the observed degenerate paired contingency (see Results). Task generation, constraints, and validator. Each synthetic task encodes (i) initial_state, (ii) an intent written in operational language, (iii) explicit per‑interface constraints (allowed fields, ‘must_be_down_for_fields’), and (iv) a required_sequence of safe steps. Representative task JSONs and the full SyntheticNetOpsIntentConfig_v1 suite are archived under execution/*; example scoring JSONs are in execution/scoring/ (example: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 350bfaa2...). Verifier rule set and pointer. The deterministic verifier configuration and rule file(s) used by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 are archived and referenced in execution/transformation_manifest.json (SHA‑256 ecd9236e84c744f3f0696d8fe96cbfe73968822be9aa153bf1e313f4fccc7317); the scoring outputs include validator_trace entries that show the exact validation outcome per episode. Provider calls and logging. All model calls, provider traces, per‑episode raw responses, scoring JSONs, and SHA‑256 hashes were deterministically recorded (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b...). Retry and failure policy. Up to two retries per failed provider call were allowed; no retries were required and failed_hosted_model_call_event_count=0. Analysis plan. Primary test: paired binary comparison (exact McNemar two‑sided) and paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Secondary analyses and validator↔emulator concordance checks were prespecified.

Full raw transcripts, provider traces, and SHA‑256 manifests are in execution/* (execution/raw_results.jsonl SHA‑256 43381c4b...).
sections.discussion: What the conditional null result means. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generated candidate per task evaluated for both arms), the chosen generator (gpt-5-mini, the declared model artifact execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e2...) produced verifier‑acceptable candidates for every task in the supplied synthetic task bank; therefore verifier insertion could not change acceptance counts. This yields a conditional null result: when a single generated candidate per task already satisfies the verifier rule set, inserting the verifier (with the chosen rules and one‑call repair budget) will not alter accept/reject outcomes. Design mismatch and consequences for preregistered power. The preregistration's power/MDE calculations assumed independent per‑arm generation (two independent draws per task). Because execution used shared candidates, the preregistered MDE is inapplicable to the executed contingency; we therefore explicitly document the mismatch and refrain from claims that the executed run tested the independent‑sampling estimand. Minimal deterministic recipe to test the original independent‑sampling estimand using the archived artifacts. To re‑run the archived harness under independent per‑arm sampling (the original estimand and power calculation), make the following deterministic edits to the archived execution manifest and model configuration (no new data invented): (1) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation = true in execution/execution_manifest.json; (2) set execution_contract.maximum_model_calls >= 540 to permit one generation per arm per task; (3) set a nonzero temperature in execution/model_configuration.json or supply per‑call seeds to induce sampling variability; (4) optionally increase execution_contract.maximum_repair_calls_per_task > 1 to examine bounded‑repair convergence. All path names and manifest fields referenced above exist in the released artifact bundle (see execution/*). Operational and scientific implications. Empirical GVR evaluations must make generation sampling semantics explicit: a verifier can only change outcomes if the generator produces candidates that trigger verifier rejections under the chosen rule set and budget. The experiment shows how a thoroughly archived run can produce an informative boundary condition and provide an artifactized starting point for follow‑up independent sampling experiments.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered, executed, and fully archived a paired study integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline. Under the executed shared candidate semantics, every generated candidate met the verifier rules and no repairs were invoked, producing a conditional null result (n11=270). The decisive methodological lesson is that sampling semantics (shared vs independent generation) fundamentally determine whether a verifier insertion is testable for a given paired estimand; preregistered power calculations must align with the actual execution semantics. We release the full artifact bundle and a minimal deterministic recipe to reproduce both the executed conditional run and to run the independent‑sampling experiment the preregistration originally targeted. All raw outputs, validator traces, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes are archived under execution/* and analysis/* (example artifact hashes and pointers are given in the Disclosure). We encourage future work to preregister sampling semantics explicitly, to evaluate multi‑model and multi‑verifier ensembles, and to explore richer bounded‑repair budgets using the provided reproducible harness.

Limitations and scope are explicitly declared in the manuscript and the archived limitations JSON. The authors declare no additional undisclosed modifications to the preregistered design beyond the logged execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=false decision which is recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json.
limitations: Synthetic task suite and emulator fidelity: tasks are synthetic and executed in a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet environment; production devices and multi‑vendor heterogeneity may produce different verification/repair outcomes.
Single model and single verifier rule set: only gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 were used; results are not multi‑model or multi‑verifier generalizations.

Sampling semantics vs preregistered power: the preregistered power/MDE assumed independent per‑arm sampling; the executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics, so the original power calculations are inapplicable to the observed conditional contingency.
Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate; multi‑attempt repair strategies may yield different repair success rates.
Emulator↔production gap: verifier acceptance against an emulator does not guarantee identical behavior or safety on production hardware and in operational processes.
